title: Neuroanatomy (ANA 302)
description: Organisation of the brain and spinal cord, major tracts, blood supply and ventricles, cranial nerve nuclei and clinical localisation of lesions.

topics.title: Cerebral Hemispheres and Functional Areas
topics.summary: Lobes, sulci, Brodmann areas, dominance and the effects of cortical lesions.

notes.b: The central sulcus separates the frontal lobe (precentral gyrus — primary motor cortex, Brodmann area 4) from the parietal lobe (postcentral gyrus — primary somatosensory cortex, areas 3, 1, 2). The primary visual cortex (area 17) lies around the calcarine sulcus of the occipital lobe; the primary auditory cortex (areas 41, 42) is in the superior temporal gyrus. The motor and sensory homunculi show body parts mapped in order, with the leg on the medial surface (anterior cerebral artery territory) and the face and hand laterally (middle cerebral artery territory).

In most people (almost all right-handers) the left hemisphere is dominant for language. Broca's area (areas 44, 45, inferior frontal gyrus) controls speech production; a lesion causes expressive (non-fluent) aphasia with preserved comprehension. Wernicke's area (area 22, posterior superior temporal gyrus) controls comprehension; a lesion causes receptive (fluent) aphasia with meaningless speech. The arcuate fasciculus connects them (conduction aphasia: poor repetition). Prefrontal lesions alter personality and judgement (as in Phineas Gage); non-dominant parietal lesions cause neglect of the opposite side.

topics.title: Spinal Cord and Major Tracts
topics.summary: Internal structure of the cord, ascending and descending pathways, and cord syndromes.

notes.b: The spinal cord ends at L1/L2 in adults (conus medullaris), so lumbar puncture is performed at L3/L4 or L4/L5. The dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway carries fine touch, vibration and proprioception; it ascends ipsilaterally and crosses in the medulla (internal arcuate fibres). The spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature; it crosses within one or two segments of entry and ascends contralaterally. The lateral corticospinal tract (voluntary movement) crosses at the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla and descends ipsilateral to the muscles it controls. Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesions give spasticity, hyperreflexia and an extensor plantar (Babinski) response; lower motor neuron (LMN) lesions give flaccidity, wasting, fasciculations and hyporeflexia.
k: Cord ends at L1/L2; LP at L3/4 or L4/5
Dorsal columns cross in the medulla; spinothalamic crosses at entry
Corticospinal crosses at the pyramidal decussation

notes.b: Brown-Séquard syndrome (hemisection) causes ipsilateral UMN weakness and loss of proprioception/vibration below the lesion, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature. Central cord syndrome (e.g. syringomyelia) causes 'cape-like' loss of pain and temperature over the shoulders with preserved touch. Anterior cord syndrome (anterior spinal artery occlusion) causes paralysis and loss of pain/temperature with preserved dorsal column sensation. Subacute combined degeneration (vitamin B12 deficiency) affects the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts. Tabes dorsalis (neurosyphilis) affects the dorsal columns.
k: Brown-Séquard: ipsilateral motor + proprioception; contralateral pain/temp

topics.title: Brainstem, Cerebellum and Cranial Nerve Nuclei
topics.summary: Midbrain, pons and medulla, brainstem syndromes, and cerebellar function and signs.

notes.b: The brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla) contains the nuclei of cranial nerves III–XII, ascending and descending tracts, and vital centres for respiration and circulation. Cranial nerve nuclei: III and IV in the midbrain; V, VI, VII and VIII mainly in the pons; IX, X, XI and XII in the medulla. Brainstem lesions produce 'crossed' signs: ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy with contralateral hemiplegia. Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, usually from posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) occlusion, causes ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, Horner's syndrome, dysphagia and ataxia, with contralateral body pain/temperature loss.
k: III, IV: midbrain; V–VIII: pons; IX–XII: medulla

notes.b: The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance and posture; it influences the ipsilateral side of the body. It connects to the brainstem by three peduncles (superior — mainly output; middle — input from pons; inferior — input from spinal cord and vestibular nuclei). Cerebellar signs (DANISH): Dysdiadochokinesia, Ataxia (broad-based gait), Nystagmus, Intention tremor, Slurred/scanning speech, Hypotonia; also past-pointing on finger–nose test. Midline (vermis) lesions cause truncal ataxia (e.g. alcohol); hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral limb ataxia.

topics.title: Blood Supply of the Brain and Stroke
topics.summary: Circle of Willis, arterial territories, the internal capsule and patterns of stroke.

notes.b: The brain is supplied by the two internal carotid arteries (anterior circulation) and two vertebral arteries, which join to form the basilar artery (posterior circulation). The circle of Willis links them: anterior cerebral arteries joined by the anterior communicating artery; internal carotids; posterior communicating arteries; posterior cerebral arteries (from the basilar). The middle cerebral artery (MCA), the direct continuation of the internal carotid, supplies the lateral hemisphere including motor and sensory areas for face and arm and (dominant side) language areas; its lenticulostriate branches supply the internal capsule and basal ganglia. The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital lobe (visual cortex).
k: Circle of Willis: ACA, AComm, ICA, PComm, PCA
MCA: lateral hemisphere — face, arm, speech

notes.b: MCA stroke: contralateral hemiparesis and sensory loss affecting face and arm more than leg, homonymous hemianopia, and aphasia (dominant hemisphere) or neglect (non-dominant). ACA stroke: contralateral leg weakness. PCA stroke: contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. A small lacunar infarct in the posterior limb of the internal capsule (hypertension) causes pure motor hemiplegia of face, arm and leg. Hypertension is the most important modifiable risk factor for stroke in Nigeria, where haemorrhagic strokes are relatively common.
k: MCA: face/arm > leg + aphasia or neglect
Internal capsule lacune: pure motor hemiplegia

topics.title: Ventricles, CSF and the Visual Pathway
topics.summary: Ventricular system, CSF circulation and hydrocephalus, and visual field defects.

notes.b: Cerebrospinal fluid (about 500 mL/day produced; about 150 mL present) is made mainly by the choroid plexus in the lateral ventricles. It flows: lateral ventricles → interventricular foramina (of Monro) → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) → fourth ventricle → subarachnoid space via the median aperture (Magendie) and lateral apertures (Luschka) → reabsorbed by arachnoid granulations into the superior sagittal sinus. Obstruction within the ventricular system causes non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus (e.g. aqueduct stenosis); impaired absorption causes communicating hydrocephalus (e.g. after meningitis or subarachnoid haemorrhage). Normal CSF is clear, with < 5 white cells/µL, protein 0.15–0.45 g/L and glucose about two-thirds of blood glucose.
k: CSF made by choroid plexus, absorbed by arachnoid granulations
Monro → third ventricle → aqueduct → fourth ventricle

notes.b: Retina → optic nerve → optic chiasma (nasal fibres cross) → optic tract → lateral geniculate body → optic radiation → visual cortex. Lesions: optic nerve — ipsilateral monocular blindness; chiasma (e.g. pituitary adenoma) — bitemporal hemianopia; optic tract or complete radiation — contralateral homonymous hemianopia; Meyer's loop (temporal lobe) — contralateral superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky'); parietal radiation — inferior quadrantanopia. The pupillary light reflex: afferent via the optic nerve, efferent via parasympathetic fibres in the oculomotor nerve.
k: Light reflex: II afferent, III efferent
